request: a spooky wizard school mystery where my roommate gets framed for stealing something and I have to find the real thief before dawn

brief.intent: Investigate a theft in your first term at a magic academy, gather clues and name the thief at a dawn tribunal
brief.audience: teens and adults who like cozy fantasy and whodunits

genre: branching mystery / choose your own adventure
why_its_good: State drives the plot: your house unlocks its own options (Quill reads the runes, Cinder asks the hard question, Moss starts with trust), clues are `clue_*` flags counted for the accusation, and a midnight hub lets you visit only two of three places (`visits>=2` routes every exit to dawn), so each run is a real trade-off.

Seven endings, each earned: accusing Finch routes to Case Closed only with `clues>=3` (else All Hunch, No Proof), the wrong suspect or a red herring loses, and the secret Weather Menders ending needs Quill's runes plus `trust>=2` with the friend you defended. Callbacks pay off earlier choices (nod along with Finch and Wren turns to the wall; bluff with her testimony and Finch flinches).

A complete storybook look: a gold-traced gothic arch backdrop, eight framed vignettes picked per scene through `scene_info`, a velvet button plaque, Baskerville, a minor-key triangle waltz, toasts that name each clue, and an end card that explains the score (Clues x 100 + Trust x 50 + Ending).
pitfalls_avoided: No made-up syntax: every reaction is a real feedback entry with `when` (clue gained, trust lost), using `moment`, `particles`, `shake` and `haptic`, and every builtin is called with its real arity (`get_or(list, i, default)`, `or_else(parse_int(s), 0)`, `fold(list, init, (acc, x) => ...)`).

Content keys are only ones the game's own functions read (`content_effects`, `content_needs`, `content_routes`, `content_callbacks`, `content_scene_info`), each story line fits about 28 characters and each label about 24, so no text overflows the 360-wide canvas.
The ending holds for five seconds before the win or lose screen (the fragment's `good_wins`/`bad_loses` are off and a `curtain` timer sets `verdict`), so players can read how the story ends.
title: The Stormglass Affair

request: a space opera adventure where I'm a smuggler pulled into a rebellion against an evil empire, with a big escape at the end and maybe a traitor

brief.intent: Fly a debt-ridden smuggler ship through a blockade, choose loyalty or money, spot the traitor and survive the final escape

genre: branching space opera / choose your own adventure
why_its_good: Two stats that pull against each other: loyalty (to the kid and the rebels) and heat (how wanted you are). Heat decides the final escape (`heat>=2` routes the right fork to Too Hot to Hide), a decoy you plant earlier lowers it, and the HUD and the ship AI's status line (`ledger_says()`) react as they change.

Betrayal both ways: you can sell the kid to the empire or fake the handoff, and your old wingmate is the traitor. Finding the tracker unlocks a confrontation, and at the Needle he always says 'go left', a trap you can only read right if you were paying attention. The secret Last Toll ending needs the heir reveal (scan the kid, or let the Warden scan) plus `loyalty>=2`.

A full cockpit look: chamfered cyan frames with ember corners, a starfield backdrop with nebulae and HUD brackets, twelve vignettes (hangar, blockade, comet tail, golden flagship eye, toll-gate star map, the Needle canyon), Futura, a heroic D-minor theme and zap, levelup, fanfare and powerdown moments.
pitfalls_avoided: Score means something and isn't leaked early: Loyalty x 100 + Cool x 50, plus ending points that land only when the curtain falls (`ending_points()` is 0 until `verdict` is set), so bots and players can't read the ending's worth before it plays.

Conditional choices never leave gaps or dead ends: `needs` hides a choice, the glue packs the visible ones to the top, and a path simulation confirms that every scene has 2 or more choices and that every path has 6 to 8 decisions.
Feedback stays in proportion for a story: shake and a warning haptic only when heat rises, sparkles for loyalty and discoveries, and no custom `{"action": ...}` or unknown node kinds.
title: Last Run of the Magpie

request: a messy rich-kid prep school drama where an anonymous gossip account is leaking everyone's secrets and I have to figure out who runs it

brief.intent: Survive your first week at an elite prep school, protect your reputation, collect receipts and unmask the anonymous gossip account
brief.audience: teens and young adults who love teen drama

genre: branching social drama / choose your own adventure
why_its_good: Secrets are the mechanic: tell your new best friend a fake secret, and when The Hostess posts it, an entry effect (`@2`, gated on `bait`) hands you the clue that only she could have leaked it. Rep and Secrets are stats, allies are flags, and a trap scene lets you prove it, or tip her off.

A real twist with consequences: unmasking Margo needs `clues>=3`, and also `rep>=1` or nobody cares (Right, but Unpopular). Warning her lets her vanish to Geneva first. The secret Truce ending needs both allies plus `secrets>=2`, so the patient path, not the loud one, wins big. Seven endings in all, from Unmasked to Off to the Alps (with goats).

A lacquer-and-pearls look: a striped café awning and lit townhouses in the backdrop, a pearl-string divider, pill buttons with pearls, nine vignettes (limestone steps, macarons, the post on a phone, the roof at dusk, the gala), Optima, a phone-ping tap sound, buzz for rep hits and a sly pizzicato-style loop.
pitfalls_avoided: Callbacks use data, not duplicated scenes: `callbacks` swap single lines by flag (the post shows your own fake secret, and Celeste softens if Dev vouched for you), so one scene shows three versions without copying it.
No real people, brands or franchise lines: the account, the school, its sign-off and every character are original, and the setting is the genre (prep-school gossip), not any show.
List lengths stay in step: 4 lines, 3 labels and 3 targets per scene, written one scene per row, with a `scene_names` key that maps each number to its scene id.
title: The Hostess Knows

request: a heist story game where I pick my crew and plan how to steal back a priceless egg from a crooked collector's masked party, and someone might double-cross me

brief.intent: Assemble a two-person crew, prep the night before, then pull off a masquerade heist and the getaway
brief.audience: adults and teens who like caper movies

genre: branching heist caper / choose your own adventure
why_its_good: Planning pays off later: the two crew you hire decide what opens up (Bea unlocks the roof, Nell a rehearsed getaway, Osric a fake egg and a workshop visit), prep choices set `cased` and `two_fakes`, and the vault and getaway read them. Rope past the lasers without casing the place and you play The Laser Harp.

The double-cross is foreshadowed and beatable: the briefing warns that one of the three has sold out before, Osric appears at the getaway only if you hired him (a route to a separate scene), and the secret Long Con ending needs you to have seen his second fake. The alarm meter (`Alarm ●○○○○`) and the getaway routes (`alarm>=3&!rehearsed`) make stealth matter.

A 1960s caper look: a teal blueprint-grid backdrop with a mustard-coral-mint stripe, paperclipped index-card buttons, twelve vignettes (the dossier, the blueprint, a peacock mask, soufflés, a laser skylight, a mint van, the bakery window), American Typewriter, a walking-bass loop and click, coin and buzz moments.
pitfalls_avoided: Conditional effects instead of copied scenes: 'Work the lock' is always shown, and `effects` entries with a condition make it quiet if you got inside (`inside`) and noisy if not, so no scene is left with a single button.
Stats are clamped where they change (`clamp(alarm + delta(...), 0, 5)`), so the meter and the score (Stealth x 100 + Ending) can't run out of range.
Text is written for a wide typewriter font: lines of about 26 characters and labels of 24 or fewer, checked in screenshots, so nothing clips at the canvas edge.
title: The Saffron Egg Job

request: a stupid brainrot game where you farm aura by tapping on beat

brief.intent: Tap when an orbiting spark crosses a glowing zone to stack aura and climb absurd rank titles

why_its_good: One verb (tap) with three readable outcomes: PERFECT, CLEAN or -500/-1000 aura, each with its own pop text, particles, mascot frame and a combo sound that climbs a semitone per streak (`note: "= 659.0 * pow(1.0595, combo)"`).

Skill curve built from the game's own state: each rep speeds the spark and narrows the zone toward a floor, while 8 rank titles from Certified NPC to Aura Deity give a reason to keep going and a ranked_up burst on every step.

The novelty lives in the game's own sections: a poly arc built by a function (`arc(c, w, r0, r1)`), a 3-frame mascot picked with `frame`, a fading spark trail with `repeat`, and an end card shown with `visible: status != 'playing'`.
pitfalls_avoided: Draws the zone with a `poly` node from computed points instead of inventing an `arc` or `ellipse` node kind.
Binds fragment events to game events (`lives.hit -> ghosted`, `combo.hit_good -> nailed`) instead of re-declaring `lives` or `combo` state.
Early taps only cost aura and stun for 350 ms; only letting the spark slip costs a life, so spam taps are punished but one fat-finger never ends the run.
Every content key (ranks, miss_lines, ghost_lines, end_lines) is read by an expression; nothing is dead.
title: Aura Farm

request: npc or main character game where weird situations pop up and you have to sort them super fast

brief.intent: Rapid two-way sorting of absurd everyday scenarios, against a draining plot-armor meter
brief.audience: friends sending it to the group chat

why_its_good: Fun in the first second: a big readable card, two huge buttons and swipe left or right as an alternative; the old card flies off in the direction you chose and a stamp slams in (MAIN CHARACTER ENERGY, WRONG. PLOT HOLE.).

One shared timer_bar is the whole tension: right calls refill it, wrong calls rip 1.5 s off, and `difficulty_curve` raises `drain_mult` over 50 s, so the run escalates without any new rules for the player to learn.
Scoring rewards both speed and streaks: 100 from `score` plus a speed bonus times `combo_mult`, with pitch-rising sounds and a level sting every 5 in a row.
pitfalls_avoided: Uses its own wrapped card text (`w` + `wrap: true`) instead of sort_bins, whose single 34 px line can't hold a joke-length scenario.
Two inputs (`tap_call` with no source, `swipe_call` with swipe sources) feed one `called` event, so buttons and swipes share one judging rule and the bots test both.
Content stays content: two lists of scenarios become a typed deck with `map(content_npc, s => {text: s, main: false})`, not hard-coded strings in rules.
title: NPC or Main Character?

request: goblin mode game where you grab snacks at 2am and dodge responsibilities

brief.intent: Drag a goblin around a 2 AM kitchen, grabbing pizza and dodging alarm clocks and emails across 5 named waves
brief.audience: anyone who has ever raided the fridge at 2 AM

why_its_good: A twist that flips the rules: 5 snacks in a row triggers GOBLIN MODE, and for 5 s `colliders()` returns [] while a game rule lets you eat the hazards for +25 each.
Clear structure and escalation: waves with joke names (LAUNDRY AVALANCHE, INBOX TSUNAMI), hazards that speed up each wave, a hazard-free breather between waves, and a win at wave 5.
Two hazard streams from different edges come from one fragment used twice, with a full original cast (goblin, angry alarm clock, angry email, pizza, brain-cell lives) and a 2 AM kitchen backdrop.
pitfalls_avoided: The second spawn_wave use binds every public name (`spawns -> emails`, `spawn_speed -> email_speed`, `spawned -> email_sent`, `Spawn -> Email`) instead of relying on auto-renames.
Keeps the HUD within the 3-node `hud_top` limit (lives, score, waves) and puts the custom snack-streak pips in `hud_bottom` rather than overflowing a slot.
Adds transparent circles under the pickup sprites so the bots, which only see rect and circle ops, can find the snacks.
title: Goblin Mode: Snack Run

request: rizz or flop quiz where you pick the least cringe thing to say and judges react

brief.intent: A speed quiz where you pick the least cringe of four replies and a panel of absurd judges scores every line

why_its_good: The scoreboard is the joke: three original judges (a monocled frog, a DJ cat, a robot nana) switch between neutral, hype and cringe frames and hold up score cards, with a pick from lists of reaction lines (a separate set for timeouts, using the quiz's `picked == -1`).
Escalating stakes in the game's own rules: a speed bonus from `asked_at` plus a streak bonus, multiplied by heat (x1, x2, x3 every 4 rounds), with a banner that pops on each heat change.
Correct quiz wiring: `quiz_questions`, `quiz_choices` and `quiz_answers` read content, `rounds` counts `question_done`, `lives` listens to `answered_wrong` and `score` to `answered_right`.
pitfalls_avoided: Every answer appears exactly once among its question's 4 choices, in content order; prompts are 23 characters or fewer because the quiz's question text doesn't wrap.
Static framing (the chat bubble behind the question, the judges' desk) goes in the backdrop, because the game's playfield nodes draw on top of the fragment's.
Hooks the heat-change sting to the public `round_started {index}` event instead of reaching for the quiz's private `_ask`.
title: Rizz or Flop

request: a broom racing game at a magic school where I dodge storm clouds and grab sparks

brief.intent: Swerve a broom between five lanes through a speeding night race, dodging storm clouds and runaway spellbooks while chaining sparks

why_its_good: Fun at once and harder each second: the first hazard falls at 0.7 s, and `difficulty_curve` (ease_in_out over 45 s) drives fall speed from 230 to 420 px/s, halves the spawn gap, brings in spellbooks that sway toward the next lane at 25% and double rows at 40%, before the finish lanterns at 50 s.

The score rewards nerve: sparks pay 10 + 5 x Streak with a pitch that climbs a whole step per streak (`note: "= 587.0 * pow(1.0595, min(combo, 12) * 2.0)"`), and skimming a hazard in the next lane pays a 'Whoosh +5' near-miss bonus with its own swish, particles and haptic.

A full original art set with depth: a layered night backdrop (crescent moon, aurora haze, castle spires with lit windows), drifting wisps and speed streaks that scroll with `travel`, 2-frame spellbook and spark sprites, a course-progress rail, a finish arch that sweeps down in the last 3 s, floating score pops and its own minor-key music loop.
pitfalls_avoided: Wires `combo` with `bind` (`hit_good -> point`, `hit_bad -> hit`) instead of new events; the streak bonus rule reads `combo` after the fragment's own rule has already raised it.
Keeps hazards in the game's own list and hands them to `collide` through `colliders()`; the game's `hit` rule removes the hazard near `hit_at`, so one cloud costs one life.
The rising-pitch sound is the game's own feedback on `point`, which replaces score's library pickup moment instead of playing both.
Stays within 3 hud_top nodes (lives, score, combo); course progress is a playfield rail, not a fourth HUD node (`A_SLOT_FULL`).
title: Moonbroom Derby

request: a space fighter flying down a narrow canyon shooting drones, with a big boss target at the end

brief.intent: Fly a starfighter down a narrowing canyon, shoot four waves of drones and break the Rift Core

why_its_good: A real campaign in about 30 s: `waves` (end_on 'clear', 4 waves) adds a drone type per wave (weaving scouts, homing divers, gunners firing aimed orbs), speeds the scroll and narrows the canyon. Wave 4 is the Rift Core with an HP bar and 3-orb volleys, and breaking it emits `enemies_gone` to win. Break banners ('Wave 3 incoming', 'Rift Core ahead!') pace the run.

One finger, plenty of skill: the ship auto-fires and you drag it sideways (glide mode, so it banks). A chain multiplier (+5 per kill up to x10, reset by a hit or an escaped drone) and a lives bonus on the core reward clean, aggressive play; bots scored from 225 to 2,920.

The canyon is drawn and checked by the same pure functions (`wall_l(y)`, `wall_r(y)`): scrolling `poly` walls with a lit rim and inner shade layer, so what you see is what hits you. Drone variants are frames of one sprite picked with `frame`, and the core is a 2-frame pulsing sprite with a scale pop on each hit.
pitfalls_avoided: Wall contact reuses `collide`: `colliders()` returns `[player]` while the ship is inside a wall, so walls get the same grace, particles, shake and life loss as drones, with no hand-rolled `hit`.
Bolt hits are computed with `let` before any `remove`, so the bolts and drones removed come from the same snapshot; each kill emits `drone_down {x, y}` and particles read `event.x`.
Score is the game's own `score` state plus `objectives.score`, shown as one number in hud_top, because lives + 'Score: N' + 'Wave n of 4' would be wider than the canvas.
Random rolls (`chance`, `random_float`) live only in rule effects; `canyon_cx`, `colliders` and every presentation expression stay pure.
title: Rift Run

request: an endless runner where I jump across city rooftops at night collecting letters

brief.intent: Time jumps across night rooftops, hopping vents and leaping alleys, while collecting glowing letters in arcs

why_its_good: Jump timing with depth: vents need a hop, AC stacks a higher one, alleys need you to land past the far edge, and the double jump rescues a late tap. Letters float in arcs that trace the ideal jump over each alley, which teaches the line by rewarding it.

Endless with a real fail and a real curve: `difficulty_curve` (ease_in over 75 s) takes the run from 250 to 490 px/s and widens the alleys, and three stumbles end it. In the bot gate, runs lasted 7 to 124 s and the best score was 30 times the worst.

Layered city with motion: a static far skyline in the backdrop, haze bands that drift at 0.12x, brick facades and alleys that scroll at full speed, a 2-frame running courier, `ground` role ledge, a +50 milestone every 100 m with a level sting, and a meter counter in hud_bottom.
pitfalls_avoided: Alleys go through `collide` too: `colliders()` adds the player's point while it stands over a gap, and the game's `hit` rule (`when: over_gap()`) bounces the runner out through the public `vel_y` and `player`, so a fall costs a life but never strands the run.
Two obstacle heights become one or two collider points with `fold(blocks, [], (acc, b) => concat(acc, ...))`, instead of a second collide fragment.
No `time_limit` on an endless game; `lives` is the lose path, and `playtest.progress` (score + lives + meters) tells the bots what doing better means.
Labels kept short ('Combo', max 6) so lives + score + combo fit the hud_top row at 4-digit scores.
title: Rooftop Courier

request: a cozy one-more-try game where you stack cake layers as high as you can

brief.intent: Drop sliding cake layers onto a growing cake; overhang gets sliced off, perfect drops grow it back, reach 24 layers for the cherry

why_its_good: One tap, understood at a glance: the overhang slices off and tumbles away, so every sloppy drop makes the next one harder. Perfect drops (within 7 px) grow the layer back by 8 px, chain a combo worth 10 more per step and ring a chime that climbs with the combo.

A gentle curve for a calm game: the slider speeds up 6 px/s per layer (110 to 260), the camera glides up as the cake grows, and a ruler with a 'Cherry line' shows the goal. Three dropped layers end it; at 24 layers a cherry pops on top and lives left pay a bonus.

Feedback a player can read: the sliding layer's outline turns white when it lines up, guide lines mark the top layer's edges, perfect layers keep a spinning sparkle, crumbs burst on every landing, and five pastel flavors cycle through list tokens (`$sponge[l.flavor]`).
pitfalls_avoided: Layers are drawn from engine shapes (`rect`, `circle`) so they can be any width; a stretched sprite would squash the frosting drips.
The win waits for a `topper` event 900 ms after the 24th layer, so the last point and combo bonus land before the objective is checked.
The perfect chime is one `note` with a Hz expression; jingle `notes` must be literal note names, or validation fails with E_PRESENTATION.
The drop input has a guard (`when: not built`) and a Space key source; the tap target is a transparent full-canvas `rect`, so bots and people can always hit it.
title: Cake Tower

request: a which-house-are-you quiz for my friends with a magic school vibe, so we can all post our results in the chat

brief.intent: An eight-question personality quiz that sorts you into one of four invented houses of a wizard academy and ends with a shareable crest
brief.audience: friends in a group chat comparing results
brief.competition: none: compare results (with a conviction score on the side)

why_its_good: Weighted answers (+2 to one house, +1 to a second) across four invented houses that are friend-group roles (the 2 a.m. listener, the chaos starter, the loophole finder, the snack bringer), and the reveal quotes your own deciding answer back (`Your tell: “…”`), so the result feels personal and is worth a screenshot.

Stakes without right answers: a candle drains on every question and scores conviction (answer on instinct for more points), hesitating twice puts the Lantern out (`lives` bound to `hesitated`), and a split heart (top two houses within 1 point) ends in a 'Torn between Moonwarden and Emberjack' loss that still names both houses.

Paced for people: a 1.5 s read lock per question, answers that pop and dim, crests along the bottom that glow as you lean toward them, a swinging-lantern drumroll, then a crest reveal with rays, house-coloured particles and a one-line share card ('I’m a Moonwarden 🌙').
pitfalls_avoided: Not `too_short`: the read lock, a 650 ms beat after each answer and the 1.8 s drumroll keep bot runs at 22–28 s (Muse's own quiz ended in 5 s).

Not `cant_lose`: two real lose paths (hesitation, and the Torn ending through an `{"end": "lose"}` effect), so 3 of 5 bots lose; the win is an `{"end": "win"}` effect too, never invented feedback syntax like `{"action": ...}`.
Parameters inside their ranges (`lives.count` 2 of 1..9) and `score`'s `point` really emitted (base 10 per answer, the time bonus added on top), so there's no unreachable fragment rule.
Every tap target is a transparent `rect` over its sprite, so both the hit-test and the playtest bots find the answers.
title: Which House Claims You?

request: a gossip trivia game at a fancy prep school where you guess who wrote each anonymous post, so I can challenge my roommate to beat my score

brief.intent: Read anonymous posts from a school confession wall and pick which of five original students (or the dean's corgi) wrote each, racing a friend's score
brief.audience: two friends, one challenging the other

why_its_good: Five original suspects with unmistakable voices (the queen bee's 'per my last', the lacrosse captain's secret haiku, the overachiever's 6:00 sharp, the clown's stairwell gum racket, the corgi's ALL CAPS) make every post a fair deduction, and each question keeps a confuser in the choices (a sailing brag: Sloane or Jasper? a dog haiku: Jasper or the corgi?).

Built for a challenge: `beat_target` shows 'Beat Jules: 1600' and wins the moment you pass it; `combo` streaks make a right answer worth 100 to 200, so one slip can cost the crown; three wrong calls, or 12 posts without passing Jules, lose.
Feels like a feed: each post types in with a cursor and a notification ping, then a stamped verdict ('CALLED IT' or 'IT WAS RAFI') pops on the card while the quiz tints the right and wrong answers.
pitfalls_avoided: The `quiz` fragment's question line doesn't wrap, so the game hands it blank questions (the same number as the posts) and draws its own wrapped post card, instead of overflowing long text.
A transparent blocker over the answers while a post types in gives people time to read and stops instant taps: bot runs take 18–28 s, not 5.

One score system: `score`'s `point` bound to `answered_right` plus one bonus rule (`50 * combo`), with `lives` bound to `answered_wrong` so wrong answers can lose; choices are written exactly as the answers, 4 per question, as `quiz` requires.
title: Who Posted It?

request: a daily space puzzle for our group chat, like decoding a secret message from a rebel ship

brief.intent: A daily cryptogram: three short scrambled transmissions from an original rebel crew, decoded one letter at a time before the jammer arrives
brief.audience: a group chat that plays the same puzzle every day

why_its_good: A real cryptogram, not plain hangman: each message is shown in a substitution cipher (a shuffled key where each letter becomes the next one in that order, so none stands for itself), so word shapes and repeated letters are clues; a right letter unscrambles every copy and scores per copy, so E is worth more than Q.

Three short transmissions per run, each with a new key and fresh signal bars, with deadpan payoffs ('the toaster is a traitor', 'the senate hates our sea shanties'); unknown letters flicker during a short decrypt beat, and a navigator tip (`hint`, twice per run) rescues a stuck player.
Daily and social: `daily_seed` labels it and the host's seed gives the whole Group the same three messages and keys, so scores compare fairly.
pitfalls_avoided: Losable for real: three wrong letters in one message lose (the game resets `lives`, the lives fragment's public state, on each `round_started`), and a 120 s jammer (`time_limit`, `on_timeout: lose`). Every gate seed set we tried had a losing bot, and the pro still wins.
A 450 ms decrypt beat between guesses keeps bot runs at 5–23 s, so they aren't over in a few taps, and `keyboard`'s required `key_state(letter)` returns exactly 0, 1 or 2.
Content stays parseable: every message is lowercase letters and spaces with `|` line breaks, at most 4 lines of 13 characters, so the letter grid always fits the console.
title: Static from the Driftwood Fleet

request: a pass-the-phone party game for a sleepover where we all build something together

brief.intent: Three friends take turns dropping swinging pillows onto one shared fort; every pillow stays in its builder's colour
brief.competition: co-op build with friendly per-player totals

why_its_good: One shared fort and everyone's pillows: each pillow keeps its builder's colour and initial exactly where they dropped it, so the fort is a picture of who did what, and the pass screen shows a mini fort and the last drop ('Ana: Comfy! +9') before handing over.

Easy to learn, with tension in the room: a pillow stays up while its middle is over the one below, every wobble squishes the fort narrower for the next friend, and a perfect drop fluffs it back out, so the room cheers or groans on every drop.
A co-op goal on top of `turns`' per-player totals: land all 12 and the fort reaches the ceiling for a Sky Fort bonus; three tumbles and it caves in.
pitfalls_avoided: `playtest.progress` counts score, lives and turn progress, so bots tap through the 'Pass to …' screen instead of idling on it (with plain score, Bullseye Relay's pro bot took 61 s).

An 'arms got tired' auto-drop after 5 s keeps every turn moving, points land at release so lookahead sees them, and the fall takes only 600 ms, so bot runs end in 4–17 s (13–17 s for a full fort) and about a minute for people.
Respects HUD capacity: `turns` already fills `hud_bottom`, so the team total is one extra `hud_top` text (3 of 3), not a fourth node or a `shared_progress` bar that wouldn't fit.
title: Pillow Fort Night
